scenes.text: One probe graded every major agent on MCP. Claude Code C L I passed. Grok C L I failed what you assumed was standard.

The probe is What the Harness, a compatibility field guide from Polytomic. It plants random markers in each field and asks the agent what it sees. It grades the promise of MCP, the standard that connects agents to your server: same server, same behavior everywhere.
Claude Code C L I earned its pass at MCP client version two point one point two nine six. The verdict reads: uses structured output.
Grok C L I told the model the answer twice. Duplicate output, the same fail across three observed versions.
Look at the harness, the app that connects your model to MCP servers. A tool result carries the answer as text and again as structured data, machine readable jason.
The MCP spec says a server should mirror that jason into text. Should is permission. So the server did nothing wrong. Your harness picks what the model sees: text, data, both, or nothing.
Sometimes the model sees nothing. On a structured only reply, Grok Bot and Cursor Agent C L I recorded no output at all. The payload never surfaced.

Even the protocol is a moving target. Against that same server, Codex C L I and Amp C L I negotiated an older revision. Claude Code C L I and Grok C L I got the newest, which removed the opening handshake.

Web developers lived this: browsers rendered the same page differently, so they trusted compatibility tables over the spec. The limit: browser quirks were bugs, while the MCP spec's should makes this legal.
What the Harness runs one probe server with reviewed community submissions. That is a field guide, and it stops short of a conformance suite. Each verdict covers one client version, one session.
The compatibility table, not the MCP spec, is what your agent implements. So point your harness at the probe and read which markers reach your model.
